messages.content: I want to design an incremental compiler that soundly reuses cross-module typechecking results even when edits can change overload and trait resolution. How should I understand the two requirements together?

The first requirement is correctness across edits: for each edited program, incremental compilation should match a clean build in both diagnostics and executable behavior. That includes edits that make a previously inapplicable candidate applicable or make a resolution ambiguous. The second is a reuse target: at least 95% of typechecking results should be reused for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. Reuse is valuable, but it cannot override the clean-build equivalence requirement.
Why is cross-module reuse particularly relevant to resolution?

A declaration can remain textually unchanged while an edit elsewhere affects the candidates considered for an overload or trait obligation it uses. The compiler therefore cannot treat an unchanged declaration—or even an unchanged typechecking result in isolation—as sufficient evidence that reusing its resolution is sound. The question is whether the resolution dependencies relevant to that declaration remain semantically unchanged across the edit.
Does “semantically unchanged” just mean that no dependency file was edited?

No. An edit and a semantic change are different notions. A source file might be edited without changing anything relevant to a declaration’s resolution, while an edit outside the declaration might change what can resolve there. The reuse target is phrased in terms of declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged, not declarations whose text or surrounding files are unchanged.
What if the type of a call still looks the same after an edit?

That alone would not settle it. An edit might change which overload is selected without changing the apparent type of the call, and that could change executable behavior. Conversely, a newly applicable candidate might create an ambiguity and require a diagnostic rather than a previously successful resolution. Clean-build diagnostics and executable behavior are both part of the correctness requirement.
So the compiler has to account for candidates that were not selected before?

Yes. Sound reuse cannot depend only on the identity of the previously selected candidate. It must also remain sound if an edit makes another candidate newly applicable or changes whether the resolution is ambiguous. Otherwise the incremental result could preserve an old answer that a clean build would no longer produce.
Is the same concern present for trait resolution?

Yes. The goal explicitly covers edits changing both overload and trait resolution. In either case, a declaration’s earlier typechecking result may rely on how a resolution question was answered. Reuse is sound only when changes relevant to that answer have been accounted for.
Could you give a small conceptual illustration without assuming a particular language?

Imagine an unchanged declaration containing a call. Before an edit, its resolution has one applicable candidate. After an edit elsewhere, another candidate becomes applicable. A clean build might still select the original candidate, select the other one, or report an ambiguity, depending on the language’s rules. The illustration does not choose among those outcomes; it shows why the incremental compiler must not assume the old resolution remains valid merely because the call text did not change.
And the comparison is against a clean build of the edited program, not against what the previous incremental run did?

Right. For any given edited state, the required reference is a clean build of that same state. The incremental compiler must match its diagnostics and executable behavior. Previous results are candidates for reuse, not the authority on what the edited program means.
When the goal says “match diagnostics,” does that include newly introduced ambiguities?

Explicitly. If an edit makes resolution ambiguous under a clean build, the incremental compiler must reflect that ambiguity in its diagnostics. It must also avoid retaining a diagnostic when the clean build would no longer produce it. The requirement concerns the resulting diagnostics across edits, not merely whether typechecking was attempted.
Does matching executable behavior matter separately from matching diagnostics?

Yes. A program can remain free of resolution errors while an edit changes which candidate applies. Matching diagnostics alone would not establish that the resulting executable behaves as the clean-built executable does. The goal names both as correctness conditions.
How should I read the 95% figure? Is it 95% of all declarations after every edit?

The stated target is at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. It is not stated as 95% of all declarations regardless of what an edit changes. The condition on resolution dependencies matters: a declaration affected by a semantic resolution change is not made safe to reuse by the percentage target.
Then an implementation that rechecks everything could be sound but would not meet the reuse requirement?

That captures the distinction. Rechecking can avoid an unsound reuse, but the goal also calls for substantial reuse among the declarations that remain eligible under the stated condition. The design has to satisfy both rather than achieving correctness by discarding the reuse target.
And reusing nearly everything would not help if it missed one ambiguity?

Correct. The 95% target does not permit a correctness exception. If a newly applicable candidate makes a resolution ambiguous in a clean build, retaining a conflicting cached typechecking result would violate the diagnostic requirement even if the reuse percentage were high.
Is it fair to say that dependencies have to cover more than facts that supported the old successful answer?

As a conceptual requirement, yes. To reuse a resolution soundly across edits, it is not enough to know only why an old answer was possible. The design must also account for changes that could introduce competing answers or ambiguity. That describes what soundness must protect against; it does not prescribe a particular representation for those dependencies.
I want to keep the objective clear without committing to a dependency representation yet. How would you phrase it?

Design an incremental compiler that reuses cross-module typechecking results only when doing so remains sound despite edits affecting overload or trait resolution. For each edited program, its diagnostics and executable behavior must match a clean build, including when candidates become newly applicable or resolution becomes ambiguous. Among declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged, it should reuse at least 95% of typechecking results.
Does “only when doing so remains sound” imply that every edit touching another module forces rechecking?

No. That would conflate the location of an edit with its semantic effect on resolution. The goal expressly seeks reuse for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. It calls for enough care to avoid stale answers without treating every cross-module edit as though it changed every declaration’s resolution.
So there are two mistakes to avoid: missing a resolution change and needlessly losing reuse when relevant semantics have not changed?

Yes, with different consequences. Missing a change can break clean-build equivalence in diagnostics or executable behavior. Needlessly rechecking declarations with semantically unchanged resolution dependencies works against the at-least-95% reuse target. The design problem is to preserve correctness while retaining that specified level of reuse.

I’d like to make the reuse idea more concrete. Could we cache typechecks with referenced-interface fingerprints and scoped candidate-set guards, then invalidate when applicability, ranking, ambiguity, or the selected implementation changes?

That is a proposed way to express the dependencies of a cached typecheck. A referenced-interface fingerprint represents interface information the typecheck relied on. A scoped candidate-set guard accounts for the candidates relevant to a particular resolution question, including the possibility that an edit changes which candidates can participate. If an edit changes applicability, ranking, ambiguity, or the selected implementation, the affected cached typecheck is invalidated rather than reused unchanged.
What work does the candidate-set guard do that a fingerprint of the referenced interface might not?

A fingerprint of an interface already referenced by the cached typecheck can describe a known dependency. But resolution can also change because another candidate becomes relevant after an edit. A scoped candidate-set guard is intended to protect against treating the previously referenced interfaces as the entire resolution context. It asks whether the candidate landscape relevant to that resolution has changed, not just whether the old selection still exists.
So it should not just record the winning overload?

Right. Recording only the winner would miss the case where an edit makes a competing candidate applicable or changes how candidates compare. The guard is meant to cover the relevant candidate set for the resolution question, while the fingerprints cover referenced interfaces. Those two kinds of dependency serve different purposes.
Why call the guards “scoped”?

The scope ties a guard to the candidates relevant to a particular resolution question, rather than treating every candidate change anywhere as a change to every cached typecheck. That matters for reuse: unrelated edits should not automatically invalidate declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. The proposal does not specify a particular representation for a scope.
Could an interface fingerprint stay the same while the guard detects a newly applicable candidate?

Conceptually, yes. The interfaces already referenced by the old typecheck might remain unchanged, while an edit changes whether another candidate is applicable. The guard is there precisely because checking only known, previously referenced interfaces could overlook that possibility. The affected resolution would need to be reconsidered before its cached typecheck could be reused.
And if a referenced interface changes but the candidate set appears unchanged?

The referenced-interface fingerprint still matters. The candidate-set guard does not replace dependencies on the interfaces the typecheck used. A change to referenced interface information requires checking whether the cached result remains valid; changes in applicability, ranking, ambiguity, or selected implementation call for invalidation under this proposal.
Can you distinguish applicability from ranking here?

Applicability concerns whether a candidate can participate in resolving the use at all. Ranking concerns how candidates that can participate compare under the language’s resolution rules. An edit could affect either dimension. The proposal names both as invalidation triggers so that the cache is not retained merely because the previously selected candidate is still present.
What does ambiguity add to those two?

Ambiguity is a resolution outcome that matters directly to diagnostics. A change could turn a previously resolved use into an ambiguous one, or change an ambiguous use into a resolvable one. The proposal explicitly invalidates on ambiguity changes, so an old cached diagnostic or successful typecheck is not carried forward when a clean build would produce a different result.
Is the selected-implementation check mainly about trait resolution?

It is especially easy to read it that way for trait resolution: the implementation selected to satisfy an obligation can matter to the resulting program. More generally, the proposal makes a change in the selected implementation an explicit reason to invalidate a cached typecheck. That protects executable behavior as well as the presence or absence of diagnostics.
Suppose the selected implementation stays the same but the ranking of candidates changes. Would the proposal still invalidate?

Yes. Ranking change is separately listed as an invalidation condition; it is not reduced to whether the same implementation remains selected. Keeping those conditions distinct also avoids assuming that an unchanged current winner is sufficient evidence that the cached resolution remains sound.
Likewise, is a newly applicable candidate enough to trigger invalidation even before deciding whether it wins?

Yes. A change in applicability is itself on the proposed invalidation list. Once another candidate becomes applicable, the earlier resolution cannot simply be accepted from the cache on the strength of its old winner. The compiler needs to account for the edited resolution context, which may affect ranking, ambiguity, or selection.
I don’t want “invalidate” to sound like we throw away every cached result in the compilation.

It need not mean that. Here, invalidation applies to a cached typecheck whose relevant dependencies show one of the specified changes. Referenced-interface fingerprints and scoped candidate-set guards are meant to distinguish affected typechecks from ones whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. The proposal is targeted reuse, not unconditional global invalidation.
Can the fingerprints alone establish that a candidate-set guard is unnecessary?

Not as this proposal is stated. It deliberately includes both referenced-interface fingerprints and scoped candidate-set guards. The guards address changes to the relevant candidates that may not be captured by looking only at the interfaces the old typecheck referenced. Removing them would leave the newly applicable candidate case unexplained.
Could you illustrate the distinction with a cross-module edit, without assuming a specific language?

Consider a cached typecheck for a declaration that resolves a use involving candidates defined across modules. An edit in another module might change an interface the declaration already relies on; the referenced-interface fingerprint helps expose that change. Or the edit might affect whether a different candidate belongs in the relevant resolution; a scoped candidate-set guard is meant to expose that. In either case, if applicability, ranking, ambiguity, or selected implementation changes, the cached typecheck is invalidated. The illustration does not assume a particular visibility or ranking rule.
How does this proposal relate to the requirement that incremental results match a clean build?

It is a proposed mechanism for deciding when reuse would risk diverging from a clean build. In particular, the candidate-set guards address newly relevant candidates, and the named invalidation conditions address changes that can affect diagnostics or executable behavior. The proposal states what should be tracked and when to invalidate; it does not, by itself, establish that a particular implementation has achieved clean-build equivalence.
And the at-least-95% reuse target?

Scoping the guards and tracking referenced interfaces are intended to keep invalidation focused on declarations with relevant semantic changes. That is compatible with aiming to reuse at least 95% of typechecking results for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. The proposal does not provide a measurement or claim that the target has already been met.
If a source edit changes some text but leaves the relevant interfaces and candidate resolution semantics unchanged, what would this scheme aim to do?

It would aim to preserve the eligible cached typechecks rather than invalidating them simply because text changed somewhere. The key distinction is between an edit and a change to the dependencies relevant to a cached typecheck. The fingerprints and scoped guards are proposed as ways to make that distinction for referenced interfaces and resolution candidates.
Conversely, an unchanged declaration could still need its cache invalidated?

Yes. Its own text could remain unchanged while a cross-module edit changes candidate applicability, ranking, ambiguity, or the selected implementation for a resolution it uses. In that situation, the proposal calls for invalidation of the affected typecheck, because unchanged declaration text does not imply unchanged resolution semantics.
I’m trying to avoid conflating a guard changing with an actual change in resolution. How should I phrase that?

You can say that fingerprints and guards are dependency checks, while applicability, ranking, ambiguity, and selected-implementation changes are the stated invalidation conditions. A detected change may require examining whether the cached typecheck remains valid; the proposal should not be read as a claim that every edit within a guard’s scope necessarily changes the resolution. The aim is to catch relevant changes without treating all edits as equivalent.
What is the concise statement of the proposal, then?

Cache typechecks together with fingerprints of the interfaces they reference and guards over the candidate sets relevant to their resolution questions. Across edits, use those dependencies to detect when reuse is unsafe, and invalidate affected cached typechecks on changes to applicability, ranking, ambiguity, or the selected implementation. Keep the guards scoped so changes unrelated to a declaration’s resolution need not prevent reuse.
How can candidate-set guards detect newly applicable imported trait implementations without invalidating unrelated declarations?

The guard needs to describe a resolution question, not just the implementation that answered it last time. For a declaration with a trait obligation, it should account for the imported implementations that could become relevant to that obligation under the language’s visibility and applicability rules. When an edit changes that relevant set or whether one of its members applies, the cached typecheck is reconsidered. A declaration with a different, unaffected resolution question need not be invalidated merely because it shares a module or an import context.
If the old typecheck never considered a particular implementation applicable, how could its guard know to watch for it?

It cannot rely solely on a list of previously applicable implementations. The guard has to cover the possibility that an imported implementation outside that old list becomes applicable after an edit. Conceptually, it protects the boundary of the candidate search as well as the answer returned by that search. The exact way to represent that boundary depends on the language’s rules; the soundness requirement is that an implementation cannot enter the relevant resolution unnoticed.
Does that mean guarding every imported implementation for every trait obligation?

Not necessarily. The guard is scoped to what could affect the particular obligation. An imported implementation that cannot participate in that resolution under the relevant rules should not force invalidation of its cached typecheck. But the scope must be broad enough to include implementations that could become applicable after an edit, rather than being defined only by what matched before the edit.
That sounds like a difficult balance. If the scope is too narrow, we miss an implementation; if it is too broad, we lose reuse.

Exactly. A narrow guard is unsound if it misses a newly applicable candidate. A needlessly broad guard may make unrelated declarations appear affected. The conceptual test is whether a change can alter the resolution question recorded for that declaration. If the compiler cannot establish that a change is unrelated, it must not claim safe reuse on that basis.
Suppose an implementation is already imported but does not apply to a declaration’s obligation. Then an edit makes it apply. Is that different from importing a new implementation?

They are different ways the relevant candidate landscape can change, but the guard must account for both. In one case, an existing imported implementation changes its applicability; in the other, an implementation becomes available through an import change. Either can make a candidate newly applicable to an unchanged declaration, so neither is covered by remembering only the previously selected implementation.
What would make a declaration unrelated to such an edit?

Its resolution dependencies would need to remain semantically unchanged. For example, if the edited imported implementation cannot affect a particular declaration’s trait obligation under the language’s rules, that obligation does not need invalidation on its account. The important qualification is “cannot affect”: merely observing that the declaration selected a different implementation before the edit is not enough.
Could two declarations use the same trait yet still have different guards?

Yes, conceptually. Their particular obligations and resolution contexts can differ, so an implementation change might be relevant to one and not the other. Sharing a trait name alone does not establish that both cached typechecks must be invalidated. Nor does having different-looking obligations automatically establish independence if an imported implementation could apply to both.
So is the guard attached to an import, a trait, or a declaration?

The useful unit to reason about is a resolution question within a cached typecheck. Imports and trait identities can inform which candidates may be relevant, while the declaration supplies the context in which the question occurs. Saying the guard is scoped to the resolution question avoids assuming that every declaration using an import has identical dependencies. It does not require a particular storage layout for guards.
Why not compare the selected implementation before and after the edit and reuse the typecheck if it is identical?

That comparison alone would be too weak for the proposed invalidation conditions. A newly applicable implementation can change the candidate set or ranking, or create an ambiguity; those changes matter even if a previous selection still appears possible. The guard is intended to prompt reconsideration when the resolution context changes, not merely when an old selected implementation disappears.
What if the newly applicable implementation definitely loses under the ranking rules?

That is a question for the edited resolution context, not an assumption the old cache can make. The proposal lists applicability and ranking changes as reasons to invalidate the affected cached typecheck. It should still avoid invalidating declarations for which that implementation cannot affect the relevant resolution question at all. There is a difference between a newly applicable candidate that loses and an implementation unrelated to the obligation.
Could the guard simply react to any change in the imported implementation set, then decide which declarations are affected?

That is one possible way to think about detection versus invalidation, without committing to a particular mechanism. A change may warrant checking which resolution questions it could affect; it does not follow that every declaration associated with the import must lose its cached result. The guard’s scope must support that distinction while still finding candidates that were absent from the old applicable set.
Is an implementation that was previously inapplicable a kind of negative dependency?

In a conceptual sense, yes: the old result can rely on the fact that no competing imported implementation applied in the relevant way. If that fact can change, a cache recording only positive dependencies on the selected implementation is incomplete. A candidate-set guard is meant to preserve the relevant ‘no other candidate changes this resolution’ condition across edits.
I want to be careful with that phrase. Does it mean recording every implementation that failed to apply?

No. It describes the semantic condition the guard must protect, not a requirement to store an exhaustive list of failed candidates. Whatever form the guard takes, it needs to detect changes that make an imported implementation newly applicable to its resolution question. Its representation can remain an open design choice.
How do referenced-interface fingerprints fit into this particular problem?

They cover interface information already referenced by a cached typecheck. Candidate-set guards address a different risk: an edit may make another imported implementation relevant even though it was not among the interfaces the old answer relied on. Using both reflects that a cached trait resolution depends on more than the interface of its previously selected implementation.
Could a declaration’s source remain identical and still need rechecking because of an import change elsewhere?

Yes. If that import change makes an implementation applicable to one of the declaration’s trait obligations, its cached resolution may no longer match a clean build. The declaration’s unchanged text does not establish that its candidate set or resolution outcome is unchanged. Conversely, an import change with no semantic bearing on its obligations should not automatically invalidate it.
Does the guard need to detect a new ambiguity specifically, or is detecting the new candidate enough?

Detecting that a candidate has become relevant prevents silent reuse of the old answer. The resolution can then be considered under the edited program’s rules to determine whether it is ambiguous, selects an implementation, or has another outcome. The guard should not presume that a newly applicable implementation necessarily creates an ambiguity; it must ensure an ambiguity is not missed if one does arise.
And if an edit affects an implementation’s ranking without changing whether it applies?

That is also within the proposed invalidation conditions. A guard concerned only with membership in the applicable set would not, by itself, address a ranking change. The relevant dependency is the resolution semantics for that question, including how the applicable candidates compare, so a ranking change affecting it must not pass as unchanged.
Where does the selected implementation fit if applicability and ambiguity are already checked?

It remains an explicit condition because a resolution can stay unambiguous while selecting a different implementation. Reusing the old typecheck in that situation could make incremental executable behavior differ from a clean build. The guard’s role is to help identify which resolution questions are exposed to such changes, while unrelated declarations remain eligible for reuse.
Would it be accurate to say that the goal is selective invalidation based on semantic relevance, not selective invalidation based merely on which files were edited?

Yes. File edits indicate where something changed, but they do not by themselves establish which trait resolutions changed. Candidate-set guards should connect an edit to the particular resolution questions it can affect, including newly applicable imported implementations. Declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged are the ones the design aims to keep reusable.
What should happen when the compiler cannot tell whether an imported implementation could affect a guarded obligation?

It should not reuse that cached typecheck on an unsupported assumption of independence. Soundness requires accounting for the possible effect; the reuse target does not authorize overlooking it. The design challenge is to make the guards sufficiently discriminating that uncertainty does not unnecessarily spread to declarations whose resolution questions can be shown to be unrelated.
So the question is not just whether the imported implementation changed, but whether the change can enter a particular declaration’s resolution?

Exactly. For a cached declaration, ask whether the edit can change the imported candidates relevant to one of its trait obligations, their applicability or ranking, an ambiguity, or the selected implementation. A guard that answers that question soundly can detect a newly applicable implementation without treating every declaration in the vicinity as affected.

Here’s a possible answer to the imported-implementation problem: use scoped trait/receiver-head indexes, with wildcard buckets for blanket implementations. An addition would identify affected resolution queries; we would recheck those queries and invalidate cached typechecks only when their resolution outcomes change. Does that hang together?

It hangs together as a hypothesis. The indexes would help find queries that an added implementation might affect, including queries whose previous result did not mention that implementation. Rechecking those queries would establish their outcomes in the edited context. The final invalidation decision would depend on whether a rechecked resolution outcome changed, rather than treating every query found by the index as changed.
What are the trait and receiver-head parts of the index doing?

They narrow the search for potentially affected queries. A query about one trait and receiver head need not be revisited for an addition that cannot participate in its resolution. The index would group queries and candidate additions by those relevant features, subject to the language’s actual applicability rules. It is a way to identify possible impact, not a substitute for rechecking a query that might be affected.
And why include scope as well?

Because the question concerns imported implementations: an addition matters to a resolution query only where that implementation can participate. Scope keeps the index from treating an implementation available in one resolution context as relevant to every declaration elsewhere. The hypothesis depends on using the scope that matters to candidate resolution; it does not specify how the compiler represents that scope.
Could a receiver-head index miss a blanket implementation?

That is the risk the wildcard buckets are meant to address. A blanket implementation may be relevant across receiver heads rather than belonging safely to just one specific head. If the index considered only exact trait/receiver-head entries, an addition like that could go unnoticed for an existing query. The wildcard bucket makes such additions visible to potentially affected queries.
Does the wildcard bucket mean rechecking every query in the whole program?

Not as the hypothesis is phrased. The buckets are part of scoped trait/receiver-head indexes, so a blanket-implementation addition would still be considered in the relevant trait and scope context. A wildcard broadens matching where a specific receiver head is insufficient; it need not erase every other distinction that limits which queries can be affected.
So an index match is only a reason to recheck, not proof that the answer changed?

Exactly. The index provides a conservative set of possibly affected queries. Rechecking determines whether an addition actually changes a query’s resolution outcome. Some matched queries may have the same outcome after rechecking, in which case this proposed invalidation rule would not discard their cached typechecks merely because the index matched.
What would count as a changed resolution outcome here?

The comparison must preserve what matters to the typecheck and to clean-build equivalence. A resolution becoming ambiguous, ceasing to be ambiguous, or selecting a different implementation are clear examples. The hypothesis does not define an exact outcome representation; comparing only a superficial property, such as whether resolution succeeded, would not be enough if diagnostics or executable behavior could differ.
Suppose a new imported implementation is indexed as potentially relevant, but after rechecking it does not apply. What happens?

The index has done its job by ensuring the addition was not overlooked. If the query’s resolution outcome remains unchanged after rechecking, the hypothesis calls for retaining the cached typecheck on that account. The cost of that case is a recheck of the query, not invalidation of every declaration the index initially identified.
And if the new implementation applies but an existing implementation is still selected?

The query still needs to be rechecked; the old selection alone cannot establish the edited outcome. Under this hypothesis, the invalidation decision turns on whether the resolution outcome, understood with all semantics relevant to the cached typecheck, has changed. It would be premature to conclude from the unchanged name of the selected implementation alone that the whole outcome is unchanged.
I want to keep the distinction between rechecking a query and invalidating a typecheck explicit.

That distinction is central to the hypothesis. Indexes identify queries to recheck because an addition could affect them. A rechecked query whose resolution outcome changes causes its dependent cached typecheck to be invalidated. A rechecked query whose outcome remains the same does not, by that index match alone, require its typecheck to be discarded. Queries the addition cannot affect need not be pulled into this recheck in the first place.
How does an addition get noticed if it was not in any prior candidate set?

The index must relate additions to existing resolution queries by their scope, trait, and receiver-head relevance, rather than consulting only the candidates those queries previously selected or found applicable. A newly added implementation can then point to queries it might affect. For blanket implementations, the wildcard buckets provide the corresponding path when matching a single specific receiver head would be too narrow.
Is the receiver head enough to establish that an addition cannot matter?

Not by itself in every case. The proposal pairs receiver-head indexes with wildcard buckets precisely because an implementation may cover more than one head. More generally, an index category is safe for excluding a query only if the language’s resolution rules make that exclusion sound. If the index cannot rule out an effect, the potentially affected query must be rechecked rather than silently reused.
Could you give a schematic example without assuming a specific trait language?

Imagine a cached query in a particular scope for trait T and receiver head H. An added imported implementation associated with that same relevant scope, trait, and head would cause the query to be rechecked. An added blanket implementation for T could reach it through a wildcard bucket even if it was not tied to H. An addition that cannot participate in that query’s scope or trait resolution would not, on that basis, require rechecking it. The edited resolution rules determine whether either potentially relevant addition actually changes the outcome.
Does “scoped” refer only to where the implementation is written?

The useful meaning here is where an implementation can participate in the query’s resolution, not merely where its source text happens to reside. The hypothesis is about imported implementations, so the index must respect the resolution context of the querying declaration. It leaves open how those contexts are encoded.
What if a blanket implementation is not applicable to a particular query despite appearing in its wildcard bucket?

That is compatible with the design. A wildcard bucket flags possible relevance; it does not assert applicability. Rechecking the query applies the language’s rules to decide whether the implementation participates and whether the resolution outcome changes. Allowing some false-positive rechecks is different from invalidating all of those typechecks.
Could the wildcard bucket create too much work while still being sound?

It could be broader than a more discriminating way of finding affected queries. The hypothesis trades some possible extra query rechecks for coverage of blanket-implementation additions. Whether that breadth is compatible with the at-least-95% typechecking-result reuse target is a question about the resulting reuse, not something the index idea alone proves. Rechecking a resolution query also should not automatically be equated with invalidating its cached typecheck.
How does this avoid invalidating declarations that use the same trait but are otherwise unrelated?

Sharing a trait can make them candidates for consideration, but scope and receiver-head relevance can distinguish their resolution questions. Even among queries the index identifies as possibly affected, the hypothesis rechecks first and invalidates only typechecks with changed resolution outcomes. Those are two opportunities to avoid invalidating an unrelated declaration: exclude its query when the addition cannot matter, or retain its typecheck when rechecking shows no outcome change.
What if a single declaration contains more than one resolution query?

The proposal is easiest to reason about per query: identify which questions might be affected and recheck those. A cached typecheck for a declaration must be invalidated if one of its dependent resolution outcomes changes. The presence of another, unaffected query in that declaration does not erase the changed dependency.
Is this a complete claim that the incremental compiler will match a clean build?

No. It is a hypothesis for detecting candidate additions and limiting the resulting invalidation. Its soundness would depend on the scoped indexes and wildcard buckets covering every addition capable of affecting a query, and on the recheck and outcome comparison capturing the relevant resolution semantics. Referenced-interface dependencies and other changes still need to be handled; the index hypothesis does not claim those are already solved.
Then what exactly is the proposed answer to the question about newly applicable imported implementations?

Index resolution queries by the scope, trait, and receiver head relevant to them, while providing wildcard buckets for blanket implementations that may apply across heads. When an imported implementation is added, use those indexes to find queries it could affect, including ones for which it was not previously a candidate. Recheck those queries, and invalidate the cached typechecks dependent on them only if their resolution outcomes change. That is the proposed way to detect additions without automatically invalidating unrelated declarations.

I want to turn the query-guard idea into a plan: record scoped overload and trait queries, along with wildcard buckets; after edits, replay the affected queries, invalidate typechecks with changed resolution outcomes, and retain typechecks whose relevant semantics are unchanged. Is that a faithful formulation?

Yes. It separates three steps: record the resolution questions a cached typecheck depends on; identify and replay the questions an edit could affect, including through wildcard buckets; and use the replayed outcomes to decide which dependent typechecks to invalidate. Typechecks whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged are candidates for retention. This is a plan for how to make that distinction, not a claim that it has already been implemented or measured.
Why record the queries instead of recording only their answers?

An old answer does not necessarily reveal what a later edit could change. Recording the scoped query preserves enough of the resolution question to ask it again in the edited context. That matters when a candidate that did not determine the earlier answer becomes relevant to an overload or trait resolution.
What does the scope contribute when we replay a query?

The scope identifies the resolution context in which the question must be answered. Replaying an overload or trait query without its relevant context could consider the wrong candidates. It also helps distinguish a query that an edit might affect from one that is unrelated. The plan does not prescribe a particular representation of that scope.
Are wildcard buckets part of the answer to finding queries affected by a newly applicable implementation?

That is their role in this plan. Some potential candidates, such as blanket trait implementations, may not fit a narrow match against a single specific receiver head. Wildcard buckets provide a way for an edit involving such a candidate to reach queries it might affect. A wildcard match calls for replay; it does not itself establish that the query’s outcome changed.
Does the plan use that idea for overloads too, or just traits?

The plan records both scoped overload queries and scoped trait queries. Wildcard buckets cover cases where a narrow candidate classification would miss a potentially relevant change; the plan does not specify that every overload query or every trait query uses a wildcard bucket. Both kinds of query follow the same broad sequence: identify possible impact, replay affected questions, and compare their resolution outcomes.
What exactly does “replay” mean here?

It means resolving a recorded question again against the edited program’s relevant context rather than assuming its cached answer still holds. The replay determines what outcome that question has after the edit. It is distinct from immediately discarding the entire cached typecheck: the outcome comparison determines whether invalidation is needed.
So an affected query is not necessarily a changed query?

Correct. “Affected” at the replay stage means the edit could change the answer, so relying on the old answer without checking would be unsafe. Replaying may show that the resolution outcome is unchanged. In that case, the plan does not invalidate the dependent typecheck solely because the query was selected for replay.
Could you walk through the case where an imported trait implementation becomes newly applicable?

The recorded trait query retains its relevant resolution context. An edit that could make an imported implementation applicable causes that query to be found, potentially through a wildcard bucket if a narrow match would miss it. The compiler replays the query in the edited context. Could we approach the cross-module reuse problem with differential Datalog? I’m proposing that it maintain scoped candidate sets and constraint proofs, and that we invalidate only declarations whose semantic typechecking inputs change.

After an edit, its differential updates would identify changes to those semantic inputs. Cached typechecking results for declarations whose inputs have not changed would remain eligible for reuse; declarations with changed inputs would be the ones considered for invalidation. What does “differential” contribute here?

It expresses the intention to update derived resolution information in response to edits rather than recomputing all of it from scratch. The important requirement is not merely that the update be incremental: its account of additions and removals must agree with the resolution information a clean build would derive for the edited program. The proposal does not specify a particular Datalog engine or update algorithm.
Why make candidate sets scoped?

Because a candidate’s existence somewhere in the program does not, by itself, mean it can participate in every lookup. A scoped candidate set represents the candidates relevant to a resolution question in its particular context. That gives the proposed invalidation rule a way to distinguish a change that can affect one declaration from a change unrelated to another.
Would it be enough for the set to contain the candidate selected last time?

No. A newly applicable candidate could change ranking or create an ambiguity even though the old selection still exists. Maintaining the scoped candidate set is meant to account for possible competitors as well as the earlier selection. The semantic inputs must be sensitive to an edit that introduces a candidate relevant to the query, rather than being defined only by the old answer.
Where do constraint proofs enter the picture?

They concern the constraint reasoning on which candidate applicability or resolution depends. A candidate may be in the relevant scope without satisfying the conditions for a particular query. If an edit changes those conditions or their satisfaction, the semantic input to that query may change even when its scoped candidate set does not. The proposal names constraint proofs as information to maintain, but does not prescribe their representation.
Does “proof” mean this proposal includes a formal proof that the whole compiler is sound?

No. Here, constraint proofs are the resolution-related evidence or derivations maintained by the proposed computation. Calling them proofs does not itself establish that cache invalidation is sound. To make the proposal sound, those derivations and the scoped candidate sets would have to capture every semantic input capable of changing the typechecking result.
Can you give a general example of why both kinds of information matter?

Consider an unchanged declaration with a resolution question. An edit elsewhere might make an additional candidate available in its scope; the scoped candidate set would need to reflect that. Alternatively, the relevant candidates might remain available while a change to constraints alters whether one applies; the constraint information would need to reflect that. Either possibility can require reconsidering the declaration, while an unrelated declaration whose semantic inputs remain unchanged should not be invalidated on that account.
Is a changed candidate set automatically a changed executable program?

No. A changed set is a changed potential input to resolution, not necessarily a changed final outcome. The edited resolution might still select the same implementation, or it might become ambiguous or select differently. Under this proposal, the declaration with the changed semantic input is the one eligible for invalidation; the change should not be projected onto declarations whose own inputs did not change.
I want to be precise about “invalidate only declarations whose semantic typechecking inputs change.” Does it mean invalidate on any source edit?

No. It draws the boundary at semantic inputs to a declaration’s typechecking, not at source files or edit locations. A source edit that does not change those inputs should not cause that declaration’s cached result to be invalidated. Conversely, a cross-module edit can change those inputs even if the declaration’s own text is untouched.
What if the semantic inputs change but the eventual resolution outcome stays the same?

The proposal’s invalidation boundary is phrased in terms of changed semantic *inputs*, not solely changed resolution outcomes. An unchanged eventual outcome would not erase the fact that an input changed. The proposal does not specify a further rule for recovering reuse after checking such a case; it does specify that declarations with unchanged semantic inputs should not be invalidated because of unrelated edits.
How would this account for an ambiguity introduced by a newly applicable candidate?

The new candidate must appear in the relevant scoped candidate information, and its constraint reasoning must reflect its applicability. That changes the semantic inputs to the affected resolution question, so the declaration cannot silently keep an old answer. Its edited resolution must be able to produce the ambiguity that a clean build would produce. This describes the obligation on the proposed approach, not a claim that it has already done so.
What if a different implementation is selected without any diagnostic change?

That still matters: executable behavior must match a clean build, not just diagnostics. The candidate and constraint information must expose input changes that can affect the selected implementation. A cache that compared only whether a diagnostic appeared would not meet the goal, even if its diagnostic comparison happened to pass.
Could Datalog derivations tell us which declaration depends on an edited fact?

That is the proposed role of maintaining resolution information as derived semantic inputs: connect changes in scoped candidate sets or constraint proofs to the declarations whose typechecking uses them. The proposal does not specify how dependencies are recorded or which derivation details are retained. Whatever representation is chosen must not overlook an affected declaration simply because the relevant candidate was absent from its previous answer.
Is it enough to track positive derivations for candidates that applied before the edit?

No. A declaration’s previous resolution can depend on the absence of an applicable competitor. If an edit makes one newly applicable, the affected semantic input must change even though no positive derivation for that candidate supported the previous selection. The proposal needs to account for those changes to the scoped candidate and constraint information, not only preserve evidence for the old winner.
What does the word “only” commit us to for unrelated declarations?

It commits the proposal to selective invalidation: a declaration whose semantic typechecking inputs have not changed should not have its cached result invalidated merely because some other declaration’s inputs changed. Establishing that inputs are unchanged must itself be sound. The word “only” cannot justify overlooking a dependency that a clean build would find relevant.

No measurement or guarantee for the differential Datalog proposal is supplied.

For an edited program, the incremental result would need to match a clean build of that same program in diagnostics and executable behavior. Is there a risk that an apparently unchanged Datalog result conceals a changed typechecking dependency?

The proposal does not specify those rules or prove that its representation is complete.

The computation should also avoid treating semantically irrelevant edits as changes to that declaration’s inputs. What do you mean by a negative candidate fact?

Is that the same as recording a list of all candidates that failed last time?

Not necessarily. The semantic dependency is that no newly relevant candidate can alter the query’s resolution. Why are negative facts harder to maintain incrementally than a proof for the candidate that won?

A proof for an existing answer identifies something already present. An absence can stop being true when an edit introduces a fact the old answer never mentioned. To reuse the answer soundly, the incremental computation must notice that the newly visible or applicable candidate falls within the query’s relevant search space. Otherwise an old resolution might survive despite a new ambiguity or a different selection.
Does Datalog negation itself solve that?

Not automatically. Expressing an absence as a negative condition is different from maintaining it correctly after updates. The question includes whether the relevant candidate universe, scope, and visibility relationships can be updated so that additions revoke negative facts for precisely the queries they affect. It also asks whether doing so is efficient enough to avoid excessive recomputation.
What changes when a module visibility edit is involved?

The candidate’s own definition might stay the same while its availability to a particular query changes. A negative fact that relied on the candidate being unavailable could cease to hold. Conversely, a visibility edit could remove a candidate from consideration. The computation would need to connect the edit to the resolution scopes it affects without treating every declaration in every module as affected.
Could one visibility edit affect both the candidate set and a trait proof?

It could, depending on the resolution rules. A candidate’s availability to a query and the proof of a trait obligation are related but distinct semantic inputs. The question is whether changes to either can be propagated to the queries and declarations that depend on them, including when a proof becomes possible, ceases to hold, or changes in a way relevant to the selected implementation.
What exactly counts as a trait-proof change?

At this level, it means a change to the reasoning that establishes the trait resolution a typecheck relies on. For sound reuse, the distinction must be fine enough to notice changes that affect applicability, ambiguity, or the selected implementation, even when a coarse success-or-failure result looks the same. The question does not specify a proof representation or an equality test for proofs.
Would changing the internal derivation always require discarding the typecheck?

That is not settled by the question. Some derivation changes might leave every semantic input relevant to the declaration unchanged, while others could change the implementation or resolution outcome. The challenge is to distinguish a bookkeeping change from a change that affects typechecking, rather than declaring every changed derivation either harmless or invalidating.
Could we maintain only the currently successful trait proofs?

That would leave the newly applicable candidate concern unanswered unless some other maintained information detected when an unsuccessful or unavailable alternative becomes relevant. The old result may rely on the absence of competing proofs, not only on the proof for its selected implementation. Whether differential Datalog can represent and update both sides selectively is the open issue.

A module visibility edit should not automatically force every recorded resolution query or declaration to be typechecked again if its relevant candidate and proof information remains semantically unchanged. At the same time, avoiding work cannot come at the cost of missing a candidate or proof change. The question supplies no numerical recomputation limit or measured performance result.
Is the at-least-95% reuse goal relevant to that concern?

Yes, as the broader reuse criterion: at least 95% of typechecking results should be reused for declarations whose resolution dependencies remain semantically unchanged. But that percentage is about typechecking-result reuse, not a stated upper bound on how many Datalog facts may be updated or queries examined. It cannot excuse a clean-build diagnostic or executable mismatch.

Conceptually, yes. Maintaining derived candidate and proof information is distinct from invalidating a cached declaration’s typechecking result. A computation might do work to establish that the declaration’s semantic inputs did not change. The open question is whether that maintenance work can remain selective enough in practice; no cost measurement is given here.

The old answer may have depended on that other candidate’s absence. Only if the maintained dependencies can show that it cannot affect the declaration’s relevant resolution queries or trait proofs. Being in a different file is not enough, and sharing a broad trait name is not necessarily enough to make it related. The precision of that distinction is part of what the question asks differential Datalog to provide without excessive recomputation.

No. A visibility edit can change availability in either direction, and trait-proof information may change accordingly. The incremental result must reflect the edited program’s resolution, whether that means a new candidate is considered, an old one is no longer considered, or the applicable proof changes. The question does not restrict itself to additions.

For an edited program, compare the incremental diagnostics and executable behavior with a clean build of that same edited program. A missed change could preserve an old resolution when the clean build reports ambiguity, selects another implementation, or reaches a different diagnostic outcome. Such a comparison addresses observed correctness, while the question of avoiding excessive recomputation also requires accounting for retained work.
So what is the precise unresolved question?

Can differential Datalog maintain resolution-scoped negative candidate information and trait-proof dependencies under module visibility edits, detecting every semantic change that could affect an answer while limiting updates and typecheck invalidation to the relevant declarations? A certificate cannot use unchanged index membership as its only evidence that resolution is unchanged. A bound relaxation could change one of those conditions while leaving the candidate in the same index entry. The open design issue is how to record that dependency narrowly enough to find affected questions without invalidating declarations whose relevant semantics did not change.
Why would index membership remain unchanged if an edit matters to resolution?

The index may classify a candidate by its head and scope, while its bounds determine whether it applies to a particular question. Relaxing a bound need not move the candidate into a different head or change its index membership. Nevertheless, it may alter whether that candidate is applicable, so an index-delta check alone cannot settle whether an existing certificate remains valid.
Would a certificate that records only the winner catch that?

Not reliably. The old winner may remain unchanged while a head-matched alternative becomes applicable. The certificate’s soundness also depends on its treatment of alternatives, including those previously rejected. A relevant relaxation has to prompt reconsideration of that rejection even if the index contains exactly the same candidates.
Suppose the certificate has a rejected-candidate witness. Is that sufficient?

Only if the witness is connected to the semantic condition that made the candidate inapplicable and that condition can be recognized as changed after an edit. Merely storing an old rejection does not reveal whether it is still justified. How to track and revalidate such conditions without excessive invalidation is precisely the question.
Are we looking for a dependency on candidate constraints, then?

That is a natural kind of dependency to consider. For each recorded resolution question, the certificate might need to depend on the applicability-relevant constraints of its head-matched alternatives, not just on the membership of the candidate index. The dependency must be tied to the questions those constraints could affect; a change to an unrelated candidate’s bounds should not automatically invalidate other declarations.
Does ‘head-matched’ mean the alternative was already applicable?

No. Head matching can identify an alternative worth considering without establishing that it satisfies its bounds for this query. That distinction is central here: a previously rejected, head-matched alternative could become applicable after its bound is relaxed, without changing the head used for index membership.

That would be broader than the question calls for. A bound edit may warrant checking resolution questions it could affect, but possible relevance is not the same as a changed resolution outcome. Declarations whose semantic typechecking inputs are unaffected should remain reusable. The challenge is to distinguish a prompt for revalidation from a decision to discard a cached typecheck.

Conceptually, the compiler would first notice that a condition supporting a certificate’s rejection of an alternative may have changed. It would then revalidate the relevant resolution question under the edited conditions. If the semantic resolution result and the declaration’s other relevant dependencies remain unchanged, that check need not cost the declaration its cached typechecking result. This is a possible pattern for reasoning about the question, not a specified implementation.
If the relaxed candidate becomes applicable, is the certificate automatically invalid?

It cannot be accepted on the basis of the old rejection. Applicability has changed, so the affected resolution must be considered under the edited program’s rules. Whether it creates an ambiguity, changes the selected implementation, or leaves some other aspect of the outcome unchanged cannot be inferred just from the relaxation. The certificate must reflect whatever outcome a clean build would reach.
What if the candidate remains inapplicable after the relaxation?

Then a check may establish that the old rejection still holds for that particular question. That distinction helps avoid invalidating declarations merely because a potentially relevant condition changed.

One whose semantic typechecking inputs cannot be changed by the bound relaxation, or whose relevant resolution assumptions remain valid after any necessary check. No. A newly applicable alternative can affect ambiguity and therefore diagnostics, even if an earlier winner is still present. The revalidation has to consider the complete resolution outcome relevant to the certificate, not just whether the previous winner can still be found.

In a conceptual sense. The earlier certificate may rely on the fact that a head-matched alternative does not apply. Relaxing its bound could revoke that fact.
